newsitem.title: UK: Free markets key to more Interconnector gas deals.
newsitem.headline: Free markets key to more Interconnector gas deals.

text.p: Further liberalisation of Europe's gas markets is needed if more deals are to follow Wednesday's agreement announced between the U.K.'s Centrica, and Thyssengas GmbH of Germany to supply North Sea gas through the Interconnector pipeline, analysts said.

"The sticking point is the liberalisation of continental markets," said Ben Hollins, energy analyst at consultants Wood Mackenzie. "The difficulty is getting third party access (to pipeline networks)."
Without third party access, sellers can only sell gas to existing pipeline users, limiting their potential customer base.
Centrica, the recently demerged supply arm of former British Gas Plc, has agreed to supply Thyssengas with three billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas, spread over seven years.

A Centrica spokesman declined to give the exact rate at which gas will be delivered, but said it would start at a low level, rising gradually to reach a plateau which will be maintained for the last three years of the contract.
Before the demerger, British Gas held a 40 percent stake in the Interconnector, but this has now passed to BG Plc. Centrica is leasing capacity on the pipeline, the first time this has been done.

This is the fourth deal to be concluded for delivery through the Interconnector, a 235-km, 40-inch pipeline which will connect Bacton on the east coast of England with Zeebrugge in Belgium, and will deliver up to 20 bcm a year of gas. Completion of the line is due by October 1998, after which Britain's gas reserves and pipeline grid will be connected with the grids of continental Europe for the first time.

Deals signed so far are between Conoco and German distributor Wingas, for one bcm a year over 10 years; between British Gas, although since the demerger the contract has passed to BG, and Wingas, for 20 bcm over 10 years; and between British Petroleum and Germany's Ruhrgas, for 15 bcm over 15 years. Assuming these are all delivered at a constant rate, even after Wednesday's Centrica-Thyssengas deal only slightly over four bcm, or less than a quarter of capacity, will be used.

But Wood Mackenzie's Hollins was not surprised that so little volume has been contracted yet. "Bear in mind the continent isn't liberalised as the U.K. is yet, although there are moves afoot," he said.
He added that because of the lack of market liberalisation, it is difficult to negotiate third party access to pipelines.

"I think there are a number of other deals under way at the moment," he said. "A lot of potential U.K. sellers will be looking to supply the industrial markets directly. At the moment this is not possible."

The U.K. is currently oversupplied with gas, and as a result prices have fallen rapidly since market liberalisation started. The Interconnector is seen as a way of disposing of surplus gas, with prices expected to rise to a European average level as supplies go to Belgium and are then consumed elsewhere in Europe.

But there is a large potential oversupply throughout Europe, with incremental volumes coming from Russia, Norway and Algeria as well as from Britain and from existing suppliers such as the Netherlands. Many analysts believe it is only a matter of time before the flow of the Interconnector is reversed and supplies from elsewhere in Europe are delivered to Britain. Europe's consumption, excluding the former Soviet Union, was 377.1 bcm in 1995, of which the U.K. used 73.1 bcm.

The Interconnector partners are Amerada Hess (five percent), BP (10 percent), BG Plc (40 percent), Conoco (10 percent), Belgium's Distrigaz (five percent), Elf (10 percent), Russia's Gazprom (10 percent), National Power (five percent) and Ruhrgas (five percent).
